clue.text: Depressed staying indoors, without being arty-farty

parts.note: someone depressed is feeling down
someone staying indoors is at home

explanation.surface: A gloomy stay-at-home who wants nothing to do with pretentious culture.
explanation.definitionFit: Down-home describes plain, homely, unpretentious ways, the opposite of affected artiness.

clue.text: Supported being brought up not to drink too much

indicators.note: in a down clue, bringing a word up means reading it from the bottom, so backwards
the word for drink is taken away, the clue saying it is not to be there

parts.note: to sup is to drink, a sip of liquid

explanation.surface: Someone raised by parents who taught moderation in drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not to drink' strips SUP from SUPPORTED, leaving PORTED, and 'being brought up' reads that upwards as the French phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase means superfluous or unwanted, more than is needed, borrowed into English.

clue.text: Went round showing injury

definitions.meaning: past tense of wind, as a road or a clock spring goes round
a cut or gash in the body

explanation.surface: Someone circled about and turned out to be hurt.
explanation.definitionFit: The two senses are spelt alike but sound different: past of wind, and a bodily hurt.

clue.text: Old soldier with burning desire to go outside

indicators.note: one word is told to go round the other, enclosing it

parts.note: a desire is a hope
something burning is lit

explanation.surface: A veteran fighter consumed by a longing to get out of doors.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoplite was a heavily armed foot soldier of ancient Greece, so a soldier of old.

clue.text: Period of Pharaohs, with family buried in gold, dimmed in recollection

indicators.note: the family is put inside the rearranged letters, like treasure underground
re-collection read as collecting the letters again in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
your kin are your family

explanation.surface: Egyptian royal history, golden tombs and family burials, half-remembered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in recollection' (re-collected) rearranges GOLD and DIMMED into MIDDLEGDOM, and 'buried in' sets KIN inside that.
explanation.definitionFit: Egyptologists name an era of ancient Egyptian history, about 2050-1650 BC, the Middle Kingdom.

clue.text: Make harder, or soften?

definitions.meaning: to harden steel or glass by heating and cooling it
to moderate or tone something down

explanation.surface: A puzzled question: does this process harden things or soften them?
explanation.definitionFit: The verb has both senses: toughening metal by heat treatment and moderating a harsh thing.

clue.text: Preferring the best by miles '-- excited about it

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go round the other piece
excited letters are stirred up into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who prefers the best by a long way, and is thrilled about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Preferring the best' is a gerund standing for the noun: elitism is that preference. 'excited' shuffles MILES to ELISM, which 'about' wraps round IT.
explanation.definitionFit: Elitism is the belief in or favouring of a select superior group, preferring the best people.

clue.text: Bringing, members into play after signal failure

definitions.text: Bringing, members into play after signal failure

parts.words: Bringing, members into play after signal failure
parts.note: when traffic lights fail, a police officer stands at a junction and directs the traffic using their arms, the members brought into play

explanation.surface: A football manager brings players on after a breakdown in communication.
explanation.walkthrough: Members here are limbs, not club members; the signal is a traffic light.
explanation.definitionFit: Point duty is a police officer's job of standing at a fixed spot directing traffic by hand.

clue.text: National winner in dressmaking competition

definitions.meaning: ... won the Grand National, Britain's famous steeplechase, in 1976
the clothing and fashion business, informally

explanation.surface: A national champion at a dressmaking contest.
explanation.walkthrough: The Grand National is a famous horse race run at Aintree; 'National' points to its 1976 winner, not a country.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally the clothes-making industry is called the rag trade, rags being clothes.

clue.text: Used best suit, maybe pricier, but not properly designed

parts.note: in card games, playing the trump suit, the highest-ranking, is to have trumped
prices that are higher have gone up

explanation.surface: A card player plays trumps, perhaps expensively, though the plan was poorly made.
explanation.definitionFit: A trumped-up charge is fabricated, invented falsely rather than honestly devised.

clue.text: Drama, rather obscure, is shown to be tantalising

parts.note: a drama is a play
something rather obscure is difficult to grasp, hard to get

explanation.surface: A rather obscure play turns out to be a tease.
explanation.definitionFit: To feign lack of interest so as to tease and attract an admirer is to tantalise them.

clue.text: Not at first cutting up a piece of cake?

indicators.note: the first letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: cutting food up into cubes is dicing it

explanation.surface: Advice on how not to start slicing a cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a piece of cake' is not 'easy' here but literally a part of the cake, the sugary coating; hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The sugary coating on top forms part of a cake, so a part of it, as the question mark allows.

clue.text: Met, perhaps, having previously settled score

parts.note: something long established or settled in the past is old
a score is a tally or account to pay, a bill

explanation.surface: Someone met, having already paid a debt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Met' is not the past of meet but the Metropolitan Police of London; Old Bill is British slang for the police.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Bill is British slang for the police, of which London's Met is one force.

clue.text: I'm given a part in pilot programme

definitions.text: I'm given a part in pilot programme

parts.words: I'm given a part in pilot programme
parts.note: read as an actor cast in a pilot episode of a television show, but pilot is the role: a flyer

explanation.surface: An actor announces being cast in the trial episode of a new series.
explanation.definitionFit: An aviator is an airman, a pilot of aircraft, which is the part the speaker plays.

clue.text: End restrictive practice in the plastics industry?

definitions.text: End restrictive practice in the plastics industry?

parts.words: End restrictive practice in the plastics industry?
parts.note: taken literally, smashing the forming shape in a plastics factory; figuratively, ending a rigid convention

explanation.surface: Reformers want to abolish a hidebound working rule at plastics factories.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to do something entirely new, ending a conventional pattern, as if smashing a cast.

clue.text: Feeling sad, sing country music

parts.note: feeling sad is feeling blue
slang for informing on someone to the police, as is to grass

explanation.surface: A melancholy singer belts out country songs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sing' and 'grass' both mean inform to the police in British criminal slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Bluegrass is a style of American country music from Kentucky, with banjo and fiddle.

clue.text: That may be investigated heartlessly, most likely

indicators.note: the central letter of the word is taken away, its heart

parts.note: something that may be investigated can be probed

explanation.surface: A case that will most likely be looked into, though coldly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartlessly' removes the middle E of PROBEABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A probable outcome is the likeliest one, the one most expected to happen.

clue.text: Not even with money could it be crude but effective

parts.note: a surface that is not even is rough
and means together with
the ready is British slang for cash, as in readies

explanation.surface: Asking whether an uneven deal, even with cash, could work in a crude way.
explanation.definitionFit: Rough-and-ready describes something makeshift and unrefined that nonetheless does the job.

clue.text: Stop travelling overseas

parts.note: read as giving up foreign holidays, but meaning to halt a ship at sea

explanation.surface: Advice to give up holidays abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors bring a vessel to a standstill at sea by setting the sails or helm to halt it.

clue.text: As a rule, discussing charge

indicators.note: discussing means talking, so the words are heard rather than read

parts.note: a period of rule is a reign

explanation.surface: Discussing a criminal charge, as is usual.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As a rule' looks like the idiom for usually; 'As' is the link and 'a rule' gives A REIGN.
explanation.definitionFit: To arraign is to bring someone before a court to answer a criminal charge.

clue.text: Dismantle the joint, perhaps, and go straight

definitions.meaning: take apart a rolled cigarette of cannabis, undoing its roll
flatten out, as a carpet or scroll does when spread

explanation.surface: A reformed character takes apart the joint and goes straight.
explanation.definitionFit: To unroll is to undo a rolled thing, and also to open out flat and straight.

clue.text: Musicians, outstanding, censored on radio

parts.note: something outstanding is big, notable

indicators.note: radio is heard, not seen, so the word is taken as it sounds

parts.note: censored material is banned

explanation.surface: Outstanding musicians are kept off the airwaves.
explanation.definitionFit: A big band is a large jazz or swing orchestra, a group of musicians.

clue.text: Give away chance to get back into the game

definitions.meaning: to include as a free extra in a deal

definitions.text: chance to get back into the game
definitions.meaning: in football, the ball is put back into play by a throw from the touchline

explanation.surface: A player throws away the opportunity to return to the match.
explanation.definitionFit: Throw-in names both a free extra included in a sale and football's restart from touch.

clue.text: Assess recording method

indicators.note: words recorded are heard on playback, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: a method is a way of doing something

explanation.surface: Evaluating how something is to be recorded.
explanation.definitionFit: To weigh a matter is to consider and assess it carefully, as if on scales.

clue.text: Couple given added support

definitions.meaning: a pair, as in a ... of pheasants
a strut or clamp that strengthens a structure

explanation.surface: A pair receive extra backing.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a pair of game birds and a support or strengthening strut.

clue.text: VIP coming if a suitable arrangement's made

indicators.note: the letters are rearranged into a suitable new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An important guest will attend if the right arrangements are made.
explanation.walkthrough: COMING IF A is rearranged, as 'suitable arrangement's made' signals.
explanation.definitionFit: A magnifico is a grandee or person of high rank, originally a Venetian nobleman.

clue.text: Scribbled notes about university training objective?

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go round the other piece
hastily scribbled letters come out jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Hurried lecture notes on a university training course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scribbled' turns NOTES into ESTON, and 'about' puts it round U. 'training' is not coaching but taking a train.
explanation.definitionFit: Euston is a major London rail terminus, a place a train journey may aim for.

clue.text: Writer, having had shoddy literary toils rejected, left

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: toils in the old literary sense are nets or snares

indicators.note: something shoddy is badly made, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An author whose clumsy literary labours were turned down walks out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns NETS into STEN; 'shoddy' turns HAD into DHA.
explanation.definitionFit: Stendhal was the French novelist who wrote The Red and the Black.
